questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy was recently diagnosed with osteomyelitis due to Serratia marcescens. He has a past medical history of pneumonia due to Nocardia and sepsis due to Burkholderia cepacia.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate screening test?
questions.explanation: Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is seen mainly in boys (most common cause is X-linked), and the spectrum of infection is distinct, including Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, and Burkholderia, The DHR test is diagnostic and measures the superoxide production in neutrophils via the NADPH oxidase complex.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q41

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman developed meningococcemia. She had a history of systemic lupus erythematosus and had an episode of meningococcal meningitis at 12 years of age.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate screening test?
questions.explanation: CH50 Recurrent Neisseria infections are a red flag for complement deficiencies, and the past medical history of SLE is another clue toward this diagnosis. The best screening test is CH50. This is a screening test for deficits in either the classic or terminal complement pathways. It tests the functional ability of complement components to lyse antibody-coated sheep red blood cells and is sensitive to a decrease, absence, or inactivity of components in the pathway.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q40

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presented with disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection. He had a past medical history of recurrent nontyphoidal salmonellosis. Investigations: HIV Ag/Ab negative HIV VL not detected
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in the IL-12 or interferon-gamma pathway
A defect in the IL-17 pathway
A defect in the IL-21 pathway

questions.explanation: A defect in the IL-12 or interferon-gamma pathway Inherited defects of innate immunity of the IL-12 or IFNgamma pathways present with disseminated mycobacterial and Salmonella infections. In countries where Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination against tuberculosis is recommended, a common presentation of this disorder is disseminated BCG infection. Defects in the IL-17 pathway lead to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, while defects in the IL-21 pathway lead to hepatobiliary cryptosporidiosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q41

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presented with a third episode of recurrent cough along with a large amount of purulent sputum production. She was known to have common variable immunodeficiency and had multiple episodes of upper and lower respiratory infections. She was afebrile. Investigations: Chest X-ray: parallel linear opacities and a few ring-like shadows
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is an abnormal permanent dilation of the bronchi, typically on the basis of chronic destruction and inflammation caused by recurrent infections or other chronic diseases. Immune deficiencies, such as common variable immunodeficiency and cystic fibrosis, can lead to dilated bronchi. This disorder can lead to purulent sputum production and recurrent cough as well as hemoptysis. The chest imaging findings can demonstrate cystic spaces caused by bronchiectasis or the parallel linear opacities or rings as in this vignette.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q14

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man had a history of frequent skin and upper respiratory bacterial infections. Physical exam revealed silvery hair and findings consistent with Parkinsonism. Investigations: Peripheral blood smear: giant granulocyte inclusions
questions.explanation: Chediak–Higashi syndrome Although both Chediak–Higashi syndrome and Griscelli syndrome can present with silvery hair, immunodeficiency, and neurologic involvement, only Chediak–Higashi syndrome presents with giant inclusions in polymorphonuclear cells.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q42

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman was seen with recurrent skin abscesses since childhood, not accompanied by surrounding redness, warmth, or tenderness. She had also had three episodes of pneumonia, which healed, leaving air-filled cavities. On physical examination she had joint hypermobility, scoliosis, and a wide nasal base. Investigations: Absolute eosinophil count 3000/μL
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyper IgE syndrome Autosomal dominant hyper IgE syndrome manifests with recurrent skin abscesses and recurrent respiratory infections healing with pneumatoceles, as well as eczema and eosinophilia. Nonimmune manifestations include joint laxity, scoliosis, fractures, and a wide nasal tip. DOCK8 deficiency is also associated with hyper IgE and frequent infections but not with skeletal manifestations. Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome also has eczema but is X-linked and is thus mainly seen in males.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q43

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man was diagnosed with disseminated Mycobacterium kansasii infection. On examination, he had multiple warts and bilateral lymphedema of the lower extremities. Investigations: Absolute monocyte count 30/μL
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in innate immunity due to IL-12 or IFNgamma deficiency

questions.explanation: GATA2 deficiency Although patients with deficiencies of the IL-12 and IFNgamma axis and with CGD can present with disseminated mycobacterial infections, while patients with WHIM syndrome (CXCR4 deficiency) and DOCK8 deficiency can present with disseminated warts, patients with GATA2 deficiency also have monocytopenia and lymphedema.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q26

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man was diagnosed with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) after recurrent infections from the age of 5 years old. Hypoparathyroidism was diagnosed after an episode of tetanic spasms at 10 years old. At 15 years of age, he developed adrenal insufficiency.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A defect in the IL-17 axis

questions.explanation: APECED syndrome Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy–Candidiasis–Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED) or autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 is characterized by the triad of CMC, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease. CARD9 deficiency and IL-17 deficiencies can also present with CMC but lack the endocrinopathies. Patients with MCM4 deficiency, on the other hand, also present with adrenal insufficiency, while patients with DiGeorge syndrome also have hypoparathyroidism.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q26

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of headache, nausea, vomiting, neck pain, and low-grade fever. He underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for alcoholic cirrhosis 6 months prior and was on high-dose steroids for induction and tacrolimus and mycophenolate for maintenance immunosuppression. He was on secondary prophylaxis with valganciclovir for CMV syndrome. MRI brain: multiple rim-enhancing lesions along the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, corpus callosum, and cerebellum.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Perform a brain biopsy The differential for this presentation is too broad, and empiricism may lead to bad outcomes. The patient underwent a stereotactic needle biopsy of the right frontal lesion. Pathology showed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that was CD20-positive. In situ hybridization was positive for EBVencoded small RNA (EBER). A PET scan showed no activity outside of the CNS. This was a case of posttransplant primary CNS lymphoma, which carries a dismal prognosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q24

questions.stem: A toddler presented with Pneumocystic jirovecii pneumonia, following a long-standing history of diarrhea, failure to thrive, and developmental delay. Laboratory examination revealed macrocytic anemia, leucopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils, and thrombocytopenia, as well as hypogammaglobulinemia.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hereditary folate malabsorption All these conditions can present with pneumocystis pneumonia. Cartilage–hair hypoplasia can also present with macrocytic anemia and short stature, but it lacks the other features of the disease (in particular, diarrhea and neurologic involvement). CD40L deficiency is accompanied by elevated IgM concentrations, while SP110 deficiency exhibits hepatic veno-occlusive disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q27

questions.question: Fill the following table (CGD is given as example)

parts.text: Complete the table (Deficient part of immunity / Mechanism of immune deficiency) for: Properdin deficiency, Di George Syndrome, CVID

cohort_answer.text: CGD (example): Phagocytes - Deficiency in NADPH oxidase prevents neutrophils from generating an oxidative burst. questions.question: What is the most important test to evaluate the immune function of the following children, if any?

A child with his third episode of perianal abscess. Each time, the aspirate grows MSSA.

questions.model_answer:
a) 2-week-old with bullous impetigo (S. aureus), well-appearing: this is a common neonatal skin infection and does not by itself mandate an immune workup; if recurrent/severe, screen serum IgE (Hyper-IgE/Job syndrome).

questions.question: A woman is about to get TNFi for rheumatoid arthritis.

parts.text: What is the time interval recommended for her to receive inactivated vaccines prior to starting TNFi?
What is the time interval recommended for live vaccine?
Name three vaccines that could be transmitted to an immunocompromised patient when given to immunocompetent household members.

questions.model_answer:
a) Inactivated vaccines should ideally be completed at least 2 weeks before starting a TNF inhibitor.
b) Live vaccines should be given at least 4 weeks before starting a TNF inhibitor (and generally avoided once therapy is underway).
c) Vaccines whose vaccine-strain organism could potentially be transmitted from a vaccinated immunocompetent household member to an immunocompromised patient: varicella vaccine (rare transmission if a vaccine-related rash develops), rotavirus vaccine (shed in stool of vaccinated infants), and live attenuated influenza vaccine (intranasal, rare transmission).

questions.question: 22. Kid with recurrent skin infections and several episodes of pneumonia requiring hospitalization.

parts.text: What other primary deficiency can look like this
You think this is CGD, what test do you do?
What is the problem with the immune system?
CXR shows LLL lower lobe pneumonia and Kinyoun Acid Fast stain shown, what is the organism?
Treatment
What other prophylaxis do you need in CGD other than TMP-SMX

questions.model_answer:
a) Other primary immunodeficiency that can mimic this picture: Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome (STAT3 deficiency).
b) Test for CGD: dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry assay (measures neutrophil oxidative/respiratory burst); NBT test is an older alternative.
c) Immune defect: mutation in components of the NADPH oxidase complex (most commonly X-linked gp91phox) causing failure of the neutrophil respiratory burst and defective killing of catalase-positive organisms.
d) Kinyoun (modified acid-fast) stain of an LLL pneumonia in CGD: organism is Nocardia species (partially acid-fast, branching filamentous gram-positive rods).
e) Treatment: TMP-SMX (high-dose) or, for sulfa allergy/severe disease, linezolid or a carbapenem plus amikacin, guided by susceptibilities and often combined with surgical drainage.
f) Additional CGD prophylaxis beyond TMP-SMX: itraconazole (antifungal, especially anti-Aspergillus) prophylaxis, and interferon-gamma.

b) After a live vaccine, wait a minimum of 4 weeks before starting anti-TNF therapy.

questions.question: Patient with CGD

parts.text: Name and describe the deficit that results in CGD
Name 4 infection they are at risk
Name one non Infectious GI manifestation
Name one non infectious skin manifestation
Name 3 medical treatments for the patient

questions.model_answer:
a) CGD defect: mutation in a subunit of the NADPH oxidase complex (most commonly X-linked gp91phox/CYBB) causing failure to generate the neutrophil respiratory burst (superoxide/reactive oxygen species), impairing killing of catalase-positive organisms.
b) Infections at risk: (1) Staphylococcus aureus abscesses/lymphadenitis (2) Invasive Aspergillus pneumonia (3) Burkholderia cepacia infection (4) Serratia marcescens or Nocardia infection.
c) Non-infectious GI manifestation: granulomatous colitis resembling Crohn disease (can cause bowel obstruction).
d) Non-infectious skin manifestation: granulomatous dermatitis/skin granulomas.
e) Medical treatments: (1) TMP-SMX antibacterial prophylaxis (2) Itraconazole antifungal prophylaxis (3) Interferon-gamma prophylaxis (curative option: allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant).

parts.text: Complete the table (Immune Deficiency Name / Type of Defect / Explain the defect) for: CGD, Properdin Deficiency, CVID, DiGeorge

cohort_answer.text: CGD: Defect in neutrophil function, impacting oxidative burst - neutrophils/macrophages cannot destroy organisms after phagocytosis; infections with catalase positive organisms (Aspergillus, Staph, Nocardia, Serratia) - septra/itra prophylaxis. Properdin Deficiency: Complement deficiency - deficiency in alternate complement system, serious Neisseria infections. CVID: Deficiency in immunoglobulins - impaired B cell differentiation leading to no immunoglobulins, recurrent bacterial (esp sinopulmonary) infections. DiGeorge: Deficiency in number and function of T cells - defective development of pharyngeal pouch leads to thymic hypoplasia, can't produce T cells (fungal, viral, bacterial infections).

questions.question: 35. Fill the following table (CGD is given as example): | Deficient part of immunity | Mechanism of immune deficiency; CGD | Phagocytic defect | Deficiency in NADPH oxidase prevents neutrophils from generating an oxidative burst; Properdin deficiency | | ; Di George Syndrome | | ; CVID | |

parts.text: Fill in the table for Properdin deficiency, Di George Syndrome, and CVID: deficient part of immunity and mechanism of immune deficiency

cohort_answer.text: CGD (example): Phagocytic deficiency; Deficiency in NADPH oxidase prevents neutrophils from generating an oxidative burst; proph itra and septra. Properdin deficiency: Complement pathway; decreased C3 convertase stabilized by protein properdin, leading to decreased complement opsonization; DX CH50, AH50 (alternative); Tx prophylactic antibiotics and vaccines for meningococcus. Di George Syndrome: Cellular immunity; decreased T cell number or function depending on extent of hypoplasia; DX: 22q11 deletion (genetic analysis); Tx BMT and thymic transplant; no prophylaxis. CVID: Antibody deficiency; heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by defective antibody formation leading to poor response to pathogens; DX: quantitative immunoglobulins; Tx IVIG monthly, no prophylaxis.

questions.question: 4. For each medication, name the mechanism of action and infections associated with it: Rituximab, Tocilizumab, Ustekinumab (stelara), Belimumab, Abatacept, Belatacept, Natalizumab, Fingolimod, Anti-TNF, Eculizumab, IL-5 inhibitor

parts.text: Name the mechanism of action and associated infections for each medication

cohort_answer.text: Rituximab: Antibody to CD20 on B cells causing B cell depletion; associated with HBV reactivation, also CMV, herpes, parvo B19, VZV, hep C in prolonged hypogammaglobulinemia. Tocilizumab: Antibody to IL6 receptor for RA/GCA; risk of active TB, invasive fungal infx, Herpes Zoster, PJP, atypical mycobacterial infection. Ustekinumab (stelara): Antibody to IL12/IL23 for plaque psoriasis/Crohn's; serious infection with mycobacteria, salmonella, BCG from vaccine, bacterial/fungal/viral, Listeria meningitis, ophthalmic HSV. Belimumab (Benlysta): B-lymphocyte stimulator inhibitor for SLE; PML. Abatacept (Orencia): Selective T cell costimulation modulator (CTLA4 Ig blocks CD28) for RA/JIA; TB, more risk with concomitant TNFa use. Belatacept (Nulojix): T cell costimulation blocker for organ rejection prophylaxis; PTLD and PML and other serious infections (bacterial, fungal, viral, protozoal). Natalizumab (Tysabri): Monoclonal Ab against α4 integrin subunit for MS; PML. Fingolimod (Gilenya): Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator for MS, dose-dependent lymphocyte reduction; PML, disseminated HSV/VZV with multiorgan failure, cryptococcosis, atypical mycobacteria, HHV8-associated KS. Anti-TNF: Antibodies to TNF/soluble TNF receptor for RA/IBD; TB, FDA warning for legionella and listeria. Eculizumab (Soliris): Binds C5, inhibits terminal complement for PNH; increased risk of meningococcal infection, vaccinate ≥2 weeks prior to first dose. Benralizumab (Fasenra, IL5 inhibitor): alpha-directed cytolytic monoclonal antibody for severe eosinophilic asthma; helminth infection

Name 2 parasitic infections that can cause weight loss and diarrhea in CLL patients

cohort_answer.text: Most common immunodeficiency: Hypogammaglobulinemia (IgA first, then IgM and IgG); also neutropenia, decreased CD4/CD8 ratio. Parasitic infections: Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Strongyloides. Other conditions: Hyper IgE syndrome (Job's Syndrome), Common Variable ImmunoDeficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, Specific antibody deficiency (SAD), inherited complement deficiency, DiGeorge's Syndrome

questions.question: 3x3 table of Congenital Immune Deficiencies to fill in (example given: CGD - Phagocytic Defect, Oxidative Burst Impaired)

parts.text: Fill in Immune System Impacted, Immune Defect, Risk/Treatment for Properidin (X-Linked), CVID, DiGeorge's

cohort_answer.text: Properidin (X-Linked): Complement Pathway; deficiency of positive regulator of alternative complement pathway; risk - fulminant meningococcal disease, treat with vaccination + prompt antimicrobial. CVID: Humoral; hypogammaglobulinemia (decreased IgG most predominant, IgM/IgA, impaired antibody response, decreased CD4 with normal B cell, decreased mitogen proliferation); risk - recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic GI infections, malignancy, treat with monthly IVIG. DiGeorge's: Cellular immunity; cardiac abnormalities, hypoCa, hypothymus leading to T cell dysfunction, low T cell numbers with intact humoral immunity; risk - recurrent sinopulmonary infections including fungal/viral, can give live vaccines if CD8>300, high autoimmune disease rates, severe form is total thymic aplasia/SCID

questions.question: AM 23. Kid presents at 2 weeks with bullous impetigo growing S aureus - treated with no issues. Any underlying tests for immunodeficiency? (1) Kid 2 years old presents with 3rd episode of perianal abscess S aureus - any tests for immunodeficiency? (1)

parts.text: What tests for immunodeficiency in each scenario?

cohort_answer.text: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD, older kid) - diagnosed via neutrophil function testing (nitroblue tetrazolium reduction or dihydrorhodamine 123 flow cytometry). Jobs syndrome/hyper-IgE syndrome (neonate) - total IgE concentration. Other associated: HIV, severe atopic dermatitis, cystic fibrosis. Leukocyte adhesion defect (LAD, neonate) - defective chemotaxis, delayed umbilical cord separation, neutrophilia, predisposition to staph infections. CGD caused by defects in phagocyte oxidase; infections with catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia cepacia complex, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia; outside N. America also Salmonella, Neisseria, Acinetobacter); prophylaxis with Septra + Itraconazole (or Vori/Posa).

questions.question: Table of Biologics – Mechanism of Action and Associated infections:

parts.text: For Rituximab, Tocilizumab, and Ustekinumab, give mechanism of action and associated infections.

questions.model_answer:
Rituximab: anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody depleting B cells; associated infections - hypogammaglobulinemia-related bacterial infections, hepatitis B reactivation, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (JC virus), prolonged/late-onset neutropenia with associated infections.
Tocilizumab: IL-6 receptor blocker; associated infections - bacterial infections (cellulitis, pneumonia) with blunted fever/CRP response masking severity, tuberculosis reactivation, GI perforation/diverticulitis.
Ustekinumab: anti-IL-12/23 (p40 subunit) monoclonal antibody; associated infections - increased risk of mycobacterial (TB) and other intracellular/granulomatous infections, generally lower infection risk than anti-TNF agents.

parts.text: What three screening tests are recommended prior to initiation of anti-TNFa

questions.model_answer:
a) Screening tests before anti-TNF: (1) Tuberculosis (IGRA or TST plus chest x-ray) (2) Hepatitis B serology (HBsAg/anti-HBc) (3) HIV testing.

cohort_answer.text: CGD: Phagocytosis; Deficient NADPH oxidase and impaired oxidative burst

parts.text: What are three types of infections you might see more commonly in someone with Job syndrome/Stat3 mutation/HyperIg E?

questions.model_answer: Infections more common in Job syndrome (Hyper-IgE/STAT3 mutation): (1) Recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses (often 'cold', minimally inflamed) (2) Recurrent bacterial pneumonia (S. aureus, H. influenzae) complicated by pneumatocele formation and secondary Aspergillus/Pseudomonas colonization (3) Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

questions.question: Regarding CGD

parts.text: Name 2 inheritance patterns and describe which one is the most common
What is the pathophysiology / cause for CGD
Name non-infectious manifestation of the skin and GI tract
What are the 4 most common pathogens involved for CGD
What are 3 prevention interventions for CGD

cohort_answer.text: Inheritance: X-linked - more common, ~65%; Autosomal recessive (4 types, all less common than X-linked). Pathophysiology: Defect in NADPH oxidase complex, preventing phagocytes from destroying ingested organisms. Non-infectious manifestations - Skin: poor wound healing, pyoderma gangrenosum, granulomatous acne, inflammatory nodular lesions, photosensitivity. GI tract: granulomatous GI inflammation (can mimic IBD/colitis), weight loss/FTT, rarely obstruction from large granulomas. Other manifestations: pulmonary granulomas, hypersensitivity pneumonitis (mulch pneumonitis), rheumatologic (SLE, RA, IgA nephropathy), GU (strictures), ocular (chorioretinitis). Most common pathogens: Aspergillus species (2.6/100 patient-years); S. aureus (1.44/100 patient-years); Burkholderia cepacia complex (1.06/100 patient-years); Serratia marcescens (0.98/100 patient-years); Nocardia species (0.81/100 patient-years). Prevention: Genetic testing before having kids; Antimicrobial prophylaxis (TMP-SMX, Antifungal: Itraconazole, Immunomodulatory: IFN-gamma); Vaccination (BCG contraindicated, live bacterial vaccines avoided e.g. Salmonella, live viral vaccines recommended - not affected by CGD)

Pathogens: Listeria monocytogenes; Legionella; Pneumocystis jirovecii; Strongyloides stercoralis; Salmonella; VZV; Endemic fungi (histo/cocci > blasto) - in bold FDA black box. Wait time after live vaccine: >=4 weeks

questions.question: Regarding X-linked agammaglobulinemia:

parts.text: In a child of age 6 months or greater, what are TWO abnormalities on bloodwork that would suggest this primary immunodeficiency?
Name one organism in each of the following that can cause recurrent or chronic infections in patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia: i) Viruses ii) Bacteria iii) Parasites

questions.model_answer:
a) Bloodwork abnormalities suggesting XLA at ≥6 months: (1) Markedly reduced or absent serum immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, and IgM all low) (2) Absent or near-absent circulating B cells (CD19+/CD20+) on flow cytometry despite normal T-cell numbers.
b) Organisms causing recurrent/chronic infection: Bacteria - encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae (sinopulmonary infections); Viruses - enteroviruses (chronic meningoencephalitis, vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis); GI - Giardia lamblia (chronic diarrhea/malabsorption).

questions.question: You are provided a table with various primary immunodeficiencies, please complete the table with the gene defect and mechanism by which predisposition to infection occurs. We have started the table for you (example row: CGD / Phagocytosis / Inability for neutrophils to complete oxidative burst).

parts.text: Complete the table (Deficiency / Type of dysfunction / Mechanism) for: Properdin deficiency, CVID, DiGeorge

questions.model_answer:
Properdin deficiency: gene CFP (X-linked); mechanism - loss of properdin, the positive stabilizer of the alternative complement pathway C3/C5 convertases, impairing alternative pathway activation and predisposing to invasive Neisseria (meningococcal) infection.
CVID: no single gene in most cases (implicated genes include ICOS, TNFRSF13B/TACI, CD19 in a minority); mechanism - failure of B-cell differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells, causing low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and poor vaccine antibody responses.
DiGeorge syndrome: 22q11.2 deletion (TBX1 region); mechanism - defective development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches leading to thymic hypoplasia/aplasia and T-cell deficiency (with cardiac and parathyroid anomalies).

questions.question: Immunodeficiency chart. Explain impairment/consequences, infection vulnerability, diagnosis, prophylaxis for: CGD, Properdin deficiency, CVID, DiGeorge

parts.text: Complete table (Impairment/consequences, Infection vulnerability, Diagnosis, Prophylaxis) for CGD, Properdin deficiency, CVID, DiGeorge

cohort_answer.text: CGD: Phagocyte deficiency, impaired NADPH oxidase complex function; vulnerable to catalase positive organisms (S. aureus, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia complex, Nocardia, Aspergillus), recurrent PNA, abscesses, suppurative adenitis, bacteremias, SSTI; diagnosis NOBT (neutrophil oxidase burst test); prophylaxis lifelong Septra + Itraconazole. Properdin deficiency: complement factor deficiency in alternate pathway, only affects males; vulnerable to Neisseria infections (severe meningococcal disease, gonorrhea); diagnosis AH50 assay (can be normal); prophylaxis vaccination with Menactra (ACWY) and Bexsero (B). CVID: humoral deficiency (sufficient B cells but impaired antibody production); recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic lung disease, GI disease (IBD); diagnosis reduced total IgG, reduced IgA/IgM, poor response to immunization, no other immunodeficiency; prophylaxis IVIG. DiGeorge: cellular deficiency, thymic hypoplasia reduces T cell numbers (some also SCID phenotype, IgA deficiency, hypogammaglobulinemia, or SAD); recurrent URTIs, SCID phenotype develops recurrent sinopulmonary infections and chronic diarrhea; diagnosis genetic testing, FISH, microarray; prophylaxis none unless SCID phenotype (then PCP ppx +/- IVIG).

questions.question: Fill in the following table: Clinical Symptoms/Organisms | Cell Types Affected/Type of Immune deficiency | Clinical Syndrome, for: Aspergillus/S.aureus/B.cereus/Serratia; S. pneumoniae/H.flu/N. meningitidis, Campylobacter; Recurrent mucocutaneous infections/eczema

parts.text: Complete table for the three rows

cohort_answer.text: Aspergillus/S. aureus/B. cereus/Serratia: phagocyte deficiency - defective oxidative metabolism, impaired neutrophil function; syndrome = Chronic granulomatous disease. S. pneumoniae/H. flu/N. meningitidis/Campylobacter: humoral deficiency, classic or alternate pathway complement deficiency, asplenia; syndrome = agammaglobulinemia, C2 deficiency or Properdin deficiency, SCD with asplenia. Recurrent mucocutaneous infections/eczema: cellular immunity; syndrome = SCID, Wiskott Aldrich Syndrome, Hyper IgE.

questions.question: Congenital Immunodeficiency. Name most important immunologic test to be performed, if any.

parts.text: 2 week old boy with impetigo, normal CBC, culture from skin grows staph aureus. Responds to treatment.
5 year old boy with his 3rd perianal abscess drained. Blood cultures negative. Abscess cultures + MSSA. Normal CBC + diff
What are 3 effects of IVIG in a CVID patient?

cohort_answer.text: A) Diagnosis consistent with staphylococcal pustulosis - no immunologic tests needed; if recurrent, consider hyper IgE syndrome (check IgE level and genetic testing for STAT3 mutation). B) Rule out CGD -> NOBT test (neutrophil oxidative burst test). C) IVIG in CVID: reduce infection rate (81% decrease in respiratory infections), reduce severity of infections (94% decrease in severe infections), reduce hospitalizations, may slow progression of chronic lung disease (bronchiectasis), reduces antibiotic utilization.

questions.question: Infection risk in CVID

parts.text: CVID patient with GI discomfort, bloating and diarrhea? (organism)
Infections at risk in CVID

cohort_answer.text: A) Giardia lamblia. B) Pulmonary: H influenzae, S. pneumo, Staph, Mycoplasma, enterovirus (chronic lung disease: bronchiectasis, pulmonary fibrosis with granulomas, acute/chronic bronchitis). H&N: rhinosinusitis, otitis media, conjunctivitis. GI: acute infectious diarrhea (norovirus, Campylobacter, cryptosporidium, Giardia, Salmonella, H pylori, IBD). UTI: mycoplasma/ureaplasma. Joints: septic arthritis. Skin: herpes zoster, molluscum. CNS: meningitis. Systemic: bacterial sepsis especially encapsulated organisms.

questions.question: AML with lung-brain cavitary syndrome

parts.text: Name 3 pathogens and tx for each
How would you investigate (not including blood cultures)?
How would you treat if this patient is allergic to penicillin?

cohort_answer.text: Bacteria: Nocardia (TMP-SMX + Imipenem/Mero plus Amikacin if multiorgan, 6 weeks IV then PO, 2 drugs for at least a year); Rhodococcus equi (Vanco or Carbapenem + FQ/AG/macrolide/rif combination, minimum 10-14 days up to 2 months); TB (RIPE); S. aureus (Clox or Vanco); S. anginosus (Ceftriaxone); Actinomyces (penicillin G or ampicillin, IV run-in 2-6 weeks, usually >3 months). Fungi: Aspergillus (Voriconazole); Cryptococcus (Liposomal AmB + Flucytosine x2 weeks then Fluconazole); Histoplasmosis (liposomal AmB then itraconazole). Investigations: brain abscess biopsy for bacterial/fungal culture; BAL for bacterial/fungal culture and gram stain; lung biopsy; TTE. PCN allergic: Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole + TMP-SMX; to target Nocardia: Imi/Mero + Amikacin + Septra.

questions.question: Q7 (2010 PM). Scenario with immunocompromised patient who develops pulmonary symptoms, found to have lung nodules. Started empirically on PipTazo and Vanco, continues to be febrile and lung nodules are worsening. Sample taken, and gram stain shows filamentous GPB.

parts.text: A) Most likely diagnosis
B) Single most important test at this point
C) Two other aerobic gram positive rods that can cause a similar picture

cohort_answer.text: A) Pulmonary nocardiosis. B) AFB stain - modified acid-fast staining (Kinyoun stain or auramine-rhodamine fluorescent stain) can make presumptive diagnosis; Nocardia differentiated from Actinomyces by acid-fastness and aerobic growth. C) Rhodococcus equi, Gordonia.

questions.question: Regarding TNF alpha

parts.text: What is the natural function/action in normal hosts?
What are 2 most common infections in patients on TNF alpha inhibitors?

cohort_answer.text: A) Proinflammatory cytokine produced by Th1 cells/macrophages; important for macrophage activation, phagosome activation, monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation, recruitment of neutrophils/macrophages, and granuloma formation/function; required for orderly recruitment of cells leading to granuloma formation; also has direct antiviral effect. questions.question: Table of biologics: MOA and associated infections for Rituximab, Tocilizumab, Ustekinumab

parts.text: Complete table (MOA, Associated infections) for Rituximab, Tocilizumab, Ustekinumab

cohort_answer.text: Rituximab: monoclonal Ab against CD20 (B cells), marks B cells for enhanced NK cell clearance/apoptosis; associated infections Hep B, TB, PCP, PML. Tocilizumab: monoclonal antibody against IL-6; associated URTI, nasopharyngitis, may cause reactivation/exacerbation of fungal or latent infections (TB, Hepatitis B, herpesvirus, strongyloides). Ustekinumab: monoclonal antibody against IL-12; associated severe respiratory infections. Additional biologics: Alemtuzumab (anti-CD52, infectious risk CMV, PML, toxoplasmosis, adenovirus, acanthamoeba); Infliximab/Etanercept/Adalimumab/Certolizumab/Golimumab (TNF-a inhibitors, risk of intracellular infections - latent viruses, listeria, legionella, and granulomas - TB, Histo; Etanercept carries lower infection risk); Abatacept (fusion protein with CTLA-4, prevents 2nd T cell activation signal, EBV-associated PTLD risk); Anakinra (anti-IL-1, TB risk); Eculizumab (monoclonal antibody to complement C5, increases susceptibility to N. meningitidis and gonorrhea; vaccinate against N. meningitidis ≥2 weeks before therapy, or penicillin ppx for 2 weeks/duration of immunosuppression if cannot delay).

cohort_answer.text: Screening tests: TB skin test (TST); Hepatitis B sAg and cAb (guidance also suggests screening for HIV and hepatitis C). questions.question: TNF alpha inhibitors.

parts.text: Describe the characteristics and MOA of TNF alpha inhibitors
What is the natural function/action in normal hosts
Which infection is most common? Describe 4 other associated infections

cohort_answer.text: MOA: Neutralize TNF; modulate cytokine response (reduce inflammation); reduction of pro-inflammatory T-cell subsets (Th1, Th2, Th17); increase in anti-inflammatory helper and regulatory T cells; induces apoptosis of pro-inflammatory immune cells. Natural function: important pro-inflammatory cytokine crucial for formation/activation of macrophages, phagosomes, granulomas; TNF-alpha inhibition predisposes to infection by intracellular pathogens and those usually sequestered into granulomas. Most common infection: TB (classic). Other associated infections: Dimorphic fungi (histo, cocci, blasto); Hepatitis B; Listeria; Legionella; Cryptococcus neoformans; Toxoplasmosis.

questions.question: X-linked agammaglobulinemia. In a kid older than 6 months.

parts.text: Name two laboratory findings that would support diagnosis (1)
List one bacterial, viral, and parasitic infection that they are at high risk for persistent/recurrent infection (1.5)

questions.question: MOA and infxns associated with biologics:

parts.text: Rituximab
Tocilizumab
Ustekinumab (stelara)
Belimumab
Abatacept
Belatacept
Natalizumab
Fingolimod
Anti-TNF
Eculizumab
IL-5 inhibitor (mepolizumab, reslizumab)

cohort_answer.text:
Rituximab – chimeric antibody to CD-20 monoclonal antibody causing B cell depletion. Used in B cell malignancies and autoimmune d/o. Associated with HBV reactivation.
Tocilizumab – monoclonal antibody to IL-6 receptor used to treat RA/JIA. Associated with Herpes Zoster, PJP and atypical mycobacterial infection, crypto.
Ustekinumab (stelara) – monoclonal antibody to IL-12 and IL-23 to treat plaque psoriasis. Nothing specific.
Belimumab – monoclonal antibody to B lymphocyte stimulator protein that inhibits B cell survival and therefore inhibits differentiation into Ig plasma cells. Used to treat SLE. Cocci and CMV pneumonia reported.
Abatacept – CTLA-4 Ig blocks CD28 T cell costimulation, used to treat RA. No specific infections risks identified.
Belatacept – CTLA-4 IG blocks CD28 costimulation. Used in RA and JIA. No particular infection risk. Associated with PTLD.
Natalizumab – inhibits migration of leukocytes, used to treat MS, Crohn's, plaque psoriasis. Associated with PML. Withdrawn from Canadian market
Fingolimod – prevents lymphocyte movement out of lymph nodes, used to treat MS. Associated with life threatening herpes virus infections.
Anti-TNF – antibodies to TNF or soluble TNF receptor that binds TNF, used to treat RA, IBD etc. Associated with TB.
Eculizumab – monoclonal ab that binds C5 and inhibits terminal compliment activation. Increased risk of Neisseria infections.
IL-5 inhibitor (mepolizumab, reslizumab) - Risk for herpes zoster, strongyloides.

questions.question: CLL:

parts.text: What type of immunodeficiency results
Name 2 parasites that cause weight loss and chronic diarrhea in these patients
Name 4 immunodeficiencies that cause recurrent sinopulmonary infections

cohort_answer.text: A) Humoral immunodeficiency-hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG3/4 most affected, IgA sometimes); cell-mediated immunodeficiency-reduced T cell function; complement deficiency-decreased properdin and B cell complement receptors; innate immunodeficiency-decreased neutrophil counts, decreased phagocytic activity. B) Giardia lamblia (with IgA def or hypogammaglobulinemia); Cryptosporidium (also with hypogammaglobulinemia). C) CVID, SCID, CGD, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, congenital neutropenia, complement deficiency, Wiskott Aldrich, DiGeorge syndrome (also CF, ciliary motility disorders, anatomic abnormalities, nephrotic syndrome).
